title: Agrochemical and household poisons
summary: The poisons that dominate Indian ICUs: organophosphate and carbamate insecticides (atropine titration, oximes, POP scale), aluminium phosphide, paraquat, yellow phosphorus rat paste, oleander and datura, and corrosive and hydrocarbon ingestion.

topics.title: Organophosphate and carbamate poisoning
topics.summary: Cholinergic crisis: secure the airway, then atropinise fast by doubling boluses every 5 min until the chest is clear, HR > 80, SBP > 80 mmHg, axillae dry and pupils no longer pinpoint; then infuse 10-20% of the loading dose per hour. Watch for the intermediate syndrome on days 1-4.

steps.title: Recognise
steps.detail: Miosis, salivation, bronchorrhoea, bronchospasm, bradycardia, vomiting, diarrhoea, fasciculations, weakness, coma; kerosene-like smell. Plasma (butyryl) cholinesterase supports diagnosis.

steps.title: Airway
steps.detail: Left-lateral position, suction, oxygen; intubate if GCS low, respiratory failure or copious secretions. Avoid succinylcholine (prolonged block); use rocuronium.

steps.title: Atropine
steps.detail: 1.8-3 mg IV bolus; if not atropinised in 5 min, double the dose; repeat doubling until the five targets are met.

steps.title: Infusion
steps.detail: 10-20% of the total loading dose per hour; review every 15 min initially; if toxic (confusion, hyperthermia, ileus), stop for 30-60 min then restart at 70-80%.

steps.title: Consider
steps.detail: Pralidoxime 2 g IV over 30 min then 1 g/h for 48 h (Pawar regimen) in moderate-severe OP; benefit is uncertain (Eddleston 2009, Cochrane). Not for carbamates.

steps.title: Safely
steps.detail: Remove clothes and wash skin (staff wear gloves). Gastric lavage only if early (< 1 h), airway protected; no forced emesis.

steps.title: Intermediate syndrome
steps.detail: Proximal limb, neck flexor and cranial nerve weakness with respiratory failure despite atropinisation; check neck flexion power and single breath count every 4-6 h; ventilate.

doseCards.dose: 1.8-3 mg, double every 5 min until atropinised
doseCards.workedExample: 2 mg → 4 mg → 8 mg → 16 mg (cumulative 30 mg) achieves targets; infusion 3-6 mg/h
doseCards.notes: Targets: clear chest on auscultation, HR > 80/min, SBP > 80 mmHg, dry axillae, pupils no longer pinpoint. Tachycardia is not a reason to withhold atropine if the chest is wet.

doseCards.dose: 2 g over 30 min, then 1 g/h for 48 h, then 1 g every 4 h until weaned
doseCards.verify: Pawar regimen from a single Indian RCT; larger trial and meta-analysis show no clear benefit.

redFlags.text: Neck flexion weakness or falling single breath count on day 1-4: intermediate syndrome; prepare to ventilate.
Wet chest after apparent atropinisation: under-atropinisation, aspiration or pulmonary oedema.

pitfalls.text: Small fixed atropine doses (0.6 mg every 15 min) for hours: patients die under-atropinised.
Using pupil size or heart rate alone as the endpoint.

pearls.text: Atropine requirements in the first 24 h can exceed 100 mg; stock accordingly.
Many 'OP' bottles in India are mixtures with pyrethroids or solvent; aspiration of solvent causes ARDS.

nodes.text: Atropinised at 5 min (chest clear, HR > 80, SBP > 80, dry axillae, pupils not pinpoint)?
Monitor 4-6-hourly for intermediate syndrome and atropine toxicity

consultantNotes.pathophysiology: - OPs phosphorylate acetylcholinesterase; "ageing" makes inhibition irreversible (hours for dimethyl, days for diethyl compounds), which is why oximes work early, if at all. Carbamates inhibit reversibly.
consultantNotes.evidence:
- **Eddleston 2008:** practical atropine titration protocol.
- **Abedin 2012:** incremental doubling boluses plus infusion reduced mortality vs conventional bolus dosing (8% vs 22.5%).
- **Pawar 2006 vs Eddleston 2009:** conflicting oxime results.
consultantNotes.controversies: - Oximes: Cochrane 2011 found insufficient evidence; many Indian units continue them. Fresh frozen plasma, magnesium and lipid emulsion remain experimental.
consultantNotes.indiaNotes: - OP poisoning is one of the commonest causes of ICU admission and death from self-harm in rural India; monocrotophos, chlorpyrifos, quinalphos and profenofos are common agents.

quiz.explanation: Pupils no longer pinpoint is enough; aim is not mydriasis.

topics.title: Aluminium phosphide (celphos) poisoning
topics.summary: Phosphine gas causes refractory shock from myocardial toxicity, severe metabolic acidosis and arrhythmias within hours. There is no antidote: early ICU care, gastric decontamination, magnesium, vasopressors, inotropes, bicarbonate and, where available, VA-ECMO as a bridge.

steps.title: Suspect
steps.detail: Grain fumigant tablets (3 g, releasing phosphine) ingestion; garlic/rotten fish odour; vomiting, shock, acidosis. Silver nitrate paper test on gastric aspirate/breath turns black.

steps.title: Early
steps.detail: Gastric lavage with potassium permanganate (1:10,000) or coconut/paraffin oil to limit phosphine release is practised in India (evidence weak); activated charcoal; staff should avoid inhaling vomitus gases.

steps.title: Support
steps.detail: Echo-guided fluids (beware LV dysfunction and pulmonary oedema), noradrenaline, dobutamine/adrenaline for myocardial depression; correct acidosis with bicarbonate; early intubation.

steps.title: Unproven
steps.detail: Magnesium sulphate, N-acetylcysteine, trimetazidine and others are used in Indian centres; none proven in large RCTs.

steps.title: VA-ECMO
steps.detail: Myocardial toxicity is reversible over 48-72 h; VA-ECMO has been used successfully as a bridge where available.

doseCards.dose: 2-3 g over 20 min, then 1 g/h (guided by levels)
doseCards.verify: No trial-proven regimen; follow local protocol.

redFlags.text: SBP < 90 with pH < 7.2 within hours of ingestion: very high mortality; involve ECMO centre early if available.

pitfalls.text: Aggressive fluid loading in cardiogenic shock.

pearls.text: Arrhythmias and myocardial dysfunction typically resolve by day 3 if the patient survives.

nodes.text: Early lavage (KMnO4 or oil) + charcoal; protect staff
Echo-guided fluids, noradrenaline + inotrope, bicarbonate, Mg

consultantNotes.evidence: - **Gurjar 2011 (Indian ICU review):** pathophysiology and supportive care; no specific antidote.
consultantNotes.controversies: - Oil-based lavage, magnesium and other adjuncts are widely used despite weak evidence.
consultantNotes.indiaNotes: - Aluminium phosphide is a leading poison in north India (Punjab, Haryana, UP, MP) with mortality of 40-80%; sale restrictions are poorly enforced.

topics.title: Paraquat poisoning
topics.summary: A mouthful of 20% paraquat can kill. Confirm with the urine dithionite test, give activated charcoal early, avoid supplemental oxygen unless SpO2 is very low, support the kidneys, and discuss prognosis honestly; immunosuppression and haemoperfusion are unproven.

steps.title: Recognise
steps.detail: Burning mouth/throat ulcers (paraquat tongue), vomiting; then AKI and hepatitis (days 1-3) and progressive pulmonary fibrosis (days 3-14).

steps.title: Dithionite
steps.detail: Urine + sodium dithionite in alkali turns blue (dark blue/navy = high risk). Plasma level against time predicts survival where available.

steps.title: Early
steps.detail: Activated charcoal 50 g (or Fuller's earth/bentonite) if within 1-2 h; skin/eye decontamination.

steps.title: Restrict
steps.detail: Avoid supplemental O2 unless SpO2 < ~90% or for palliation; oxygen fuels free-radical lung injury.

steps.title: Kidneys and comfort
steps.detail: IV fluids for losses, dialysis for AKI (does not remove significant paraquat once distributed), analgesia for mucosal burns, early palliative care conversation if dithionite strongly positive.

steps.title: Discuss
steps.detail: Cyclophosphamide + methylprednisolone, NAC, haemoperfusion: no convincing RCT benefit; consider only within trials or local protocols.

redFlags.text: Dark blue urine dithionite test within 24 h: very high mortality.

pitfalls.text: Routine high-flow oxygen for mild desaturation.

pearls.text: Paraquat is not detected by routine toxicology screens; ask specifically.

nodes.text: Fluids, renal support, analgesia; restrict O2
Prognosis discussion; palliative care if severe

consultantNotes.evidence: - **Gawarammana & Buckley 2011:** systematic review of management; no intervention proven to reduce mortality.
consultantNotes.indiaNotes: - Paraquat (e.g. 24% SL formulations) is widely available in south and east India; some states (e.g. Kerala) have restricted it.

topics.title: Yellow phosphorus (rat paste) poisoning
topics.summary: Rat-killer paste (3% yellow phosphorus) causes a deceptive latent phase followed by acute liver failure on days 3-5. Admit every ingestion, monitor INR and liver tests daily, refer early to a liver unit, and consider plasma exchange as a bridge; transplantation for King's criteria.

steps.title: GI phase
steps.detail: Vomiting, garlic odour, abdominal pain; may be minimal. Do not discharge.

steps.title: Latent phase
steps.detail: Apparent recovery; monitor INR, bilirubin, ALT, glucose, creatinine at least daily.

steps.title: Hepatic phase
steps.detail: Jaundice, rising INR, encephalopathy, hypoglycaemia, cardiotoxicity (arrhythmias, shock), AKI.

steps.title: Support
steps.detail: ALF care (liver failure module): glucose, lactulose, ICP precautions; NAC is used empirically.

steps.title: Plasma exchange
steps.detail: TPE improved survival in an Indian series (overall 79%; all 23 patients not meeting King's criteria survived). Refer early for liver transplant assessment.

doseCards.dose: 150 mg/kg over 1 h, then 50 mg/kg over 4 h, then 100 mg/kg over 16 h; often continued
doseCards.verify: No RCT evidence in yellow phosphorus; dose borrowed from paracetamol regimens.

redFlags.text: INR > 1.5 or any encephalopathy: transfer to a liver unit now.

pitfalls.text: Discharging an asymptomatic patient on day 1.

pearls.text: Ask about 'Ratol' or similar paste by brand name; it is often mistaken as harmless.

nodes.text: Admit; daily INR, LFT, glucose, creatinine
Liver unit: ALF care, NAC, plasma exchange

consultantNotes.evidence:
- **Varghese 2020:** observational TPE series in yellow phosphorus ALF.
- **Eapen 2021:** Indian management constraints and recommendations.
consultantNotes.indiaNotes: - A leading cause of drug/toxin ALF in south and west India (Tamil Nadu, Kerala, Maharashtra); several states have moved to restrict sale.

topics.title: Plant poisons: oleander and datura
topics.summary: Yellow/common oleander seeds act like digoxin: vomiting, bradyarrhythmias, heart block and hyperkalaemia; treat with atropine, temporary pacing, potassium control and digoxin Fab if available. Datura causes an anticholinergic toxidrome: sedate with benzodiazepines, cool, and catheterise.

steps.title: Recognise
steps.detail: Seeds/leaves (Thevetia peruviana, Nerium oleander) ingestion; vomiting, sinus bradycardia, AV block, ventricular ectopy/tachycardia, hyperkalaemia. Serum digoxin assay may cross-react (qualitative only).

steps.title: Treat
steps.detail: Continuous ECG; activated charcoal; atropine for bradycardia; temporary transvenous pacing for high-grade block; treat hyperkalaemia with insulin-glucose (avoid calcium); correct Mg2+ and K+.

steps.title: Antidote
steps.detail: Digoxin Fab 1200 mg reversed arrhythmias within hours in the Sri Lankan RCT; cost limits use.

steps.title: Recognise
steps.detail: 'Dry as a bone, red as a beet, hot as a hare, blind as a bat, mad as a hatter': mydriasis, tachycardia, hyperthermia, urinary retention, ileus, delirium; often in food or drink (robbery/spiking) or seeds mistaken for chilli.

steps.title: Treat
steps.detail: Benzodiazepines for agitation, external cooling, catheterise, fluids; avoid antipsychotics with anticholinergic action; physostigmine (rarely available) for severe delirium if no QRS widening.

doseCards.dose: 1200 mg (30 vials) as in the RCT
doseCards.verify: Very costly and often unavailable in India; confirm supply.

redFlags.text: Ventricular arrhythmia or complete heart block in oleander poisoning.
Hyperthermia > 40 °C with agitation in datura: active cooling, sedation.

pitfalls.text: Giving IV calcium for hyperkalaemia in cardiac glycoside toxicity (historically feared; avoid if alternatives exist).
Restraining an anticholinergic patient without sedation (hyperthermia, rhabdomyolysis).

pearls.text: Yellow oleander self-poisoning is common in Tamil Nadu and Sri Lanka.

nodes.text: Digoxin Fab if available; correct K+/Mg2+

consultantNotes.evidence: - **Eddleston 2000 (Lancet RCT, n = 66):** digoxin Fab rapidly reversed oleander-induced arrhythmias.
consultantNotes.indiaNotes: - Oleander and datura poisonings are frequent in southern India; datura spiking of food/drinks is reported on trains and highways.

topics.title: Corrosive and hydrocarbon (kerosene) ingestion
topics.summary: Corrosives: protect the airway, no emesis, neutralisation or blind NG tube; early endoscopy (within 12-48 h) or CT to grade injury and identify perforation needing surgery. Hydrocarbons: the danger is aspiration pneumonitis; no lavage or emesis; supportive respiratory care.

steps.title: Airway first
steps.detail: Stridor, drooling, hoarseness: early senior airway management (fibreoptic/surgical airway ready); avoid blind intubation attempts.

steps.title: Do not
steps.detail: Induce vomiting, give neutralising agents or activated charcoal, or insert a blind NG tube.

steps.title: Assess
steps.detail: Erect CXR/CT for perforation (mediastinitis, peritonitis); endoscopy within 12-48 h (avoid days 5-15) with Zargar grading.

steps.title: Manage by grade
steps.detail: Grade 0-1: early oral intake. 2a: liquids, PPI. 2b-3a: nil by mouth, feeding jejunostomy/NJ, monitor for strictures. 3b (extensive necrosis) or perforation: emergency surgery.

steps.title: Aspiration
steps.detail: Cough, choking, tachypnoea within hours: CXR changes may lag 6 h; oxygen, HFNC/NIV or lung-protective ventilation; no prophylactic antibiotics or steroids. Observe 6 h; asymptomatic with normal CXR can go home.

tables.title: Zargar endoscopic classification of corrosive injury
rows: As 2a plus deep discrete or circumferential ulcers
tables.caption: Grades 2b and above predict stricture; 3b predicts perforation and death.

redFlags.text: Chest or abdominal pain, subcutaneous emphysema, fever or shock after corrosive ingestion: perforation.

pitfalls.text: Blind NG tube in corrosive injury (perforation).
Gastric lavage after kerosene ingestion (increases aspiration).

pearls.text: Acids (toilet cleaner, battery acid) injure the stomach more; alkalis injure the oesophagus more.

nodes.text: Grade 2b-3: NPO, enteral access, stricture surveillance

consultantNotes.evidence: - **Zargar 1991 (Chandigarh):** modified endoscopic grading predicting stricture and mortality.
consultantNotes.controversies: - CT is increasingly used instead of endoscopy to decide surgery; steroids to prevent strictures are not recommended.
consultantNotes.indiaNotes: - Toilet cleaners (hydrochloric acid) and battery acid are the commonest corrosives in India; kerosene ingestion in children remains common in rural homes.

drugs.name: Atropine
drugs.indications: Muscarinic features of OP/carbamate poisoning (bronchorrhoea, bronchospasm, bradycardia, hypotension); symptomatic bradycardia in oleander toxicity.
drugs.adultDose: OP: 1.8-3 mg IV bolus, doubling every 5 min until atropinised; then infusion of 10-20% of the total loading dose per hour, titrated. Oleander bradycardia: 0.6-1.2 mg IV, repeat.
drugs.preparationIndia: 0.6 mg/mL 1 mL ampoules (multiple ampoules needed); some hospitals stock 1 mg/mL.
drugs.cautions: Atropine toxicity: agitation, hyperthermia, absent bowel sounds, urinary retention – pause and restart at 70-80% of the rate.

drugs.name: Pralidoxime (PAM)
drugs.indications: Moderate-severe OP poisoning (benefit uncertain); not for carbamates.
drugs.adultDose: Pawar regimen: 2 g IV over 30 min, then 1 g/h for 48 h, then 1 g every 4 h until weaned. WHO regimen: 30 mg/kg load then 8 mg/kg/h.
drugs.cautions: Evidence conflicting (Pawar 2006 benefit; Eddleston 2009 and Cochrane: no clear benefit). Rapid injection causes vomiting, tachycardia, muscle weakness.
drugs.verify: Unit protocols vary; document which regimen your ICU uses.

drugs.name: Magnesium sulphate
drugs.indications: Aluminium phosphide poisoning (arrhythmias, hypomagnesaemia) – supportive, unproven mortality benefit.
drugs.adultDose: 2-3 g IV over 20 min, then 1 g/h guided by Mg2+ levels and reflexes.
drugs.verify: Regimens for phosphide poisoning vary between Indian centres; confirm local protocol.

drugs.name: N-acetylcysteine
drugs.indications: Yellow phosphorus and aluminium phosphide poisoning (adjunct, unproven); paracetamol overdose.
drugs.adultDose: Paracetamol-style regimen (150 mg/kg over 1 h, then 50 mg/kg over 4 h, then 100 mg/kg over 16 h) or the SNAP 12-h regimen.

drugs.name: Digoxin-specific antibody fragments
drugs.indications: Life-threatening arrhythmia from cardiac glycosides (digoxin, yellow oleander).
drugs.adultDose: Yellow oleander trial: 1200 mg (30 vials of 40 mg) IV; digoxin: by body load or 2-10 vials empirically.
drugs.preparationIndia: Very expensive and rarely stocked in India.

verify.reason: Contact a poison centre (e.g. AIIMS National Poisons Information Centre, New Delhi: 1800-116-117) for unusual agents; confirm the current number.
India has banned or restricted several highly hazardous pesticides (state-wise bans on paraquat and some OPs); local product mix changes over time.
